articles.title: LG’s RGB LED TV is good, but others do it better
articles.text:
When it comes to TVs, the LG name has long been synonymous with OLEDs, continually leading Samsung and Sony as the top OLED manufacturer. But 2026 is all about RGB LED TVs. Almost every major company has released models with the new technology — including LG and its $3,600 75-inch Micro RGB evo MRGB95B that I’ve been testing. And while LG’s RGB LED TV benefits from the brightness and color capability the technology provides, it has issues I couldn’t overlook that its less expensive competitors don’t.
LG’s RGB LED TV is good for certain situations, but an OLED is better
A bunch of little issues add up to make the MRGB95B not worth the price when competitors do it better.
The MRGB95B comes in three sizes, with the 75-inch being the smallest. It has four HDMI 2.1 ports, supports Dolby Vision — although not Dolby Vision 2 or HDR10+ — and comes with the Magic Remote design LG unveiled last year. It has a more traditional remote shape instead of the curved wand of previous versions. As with all LG TVs, the MRGB95B runs on webOS. It runs quickly, but I find it less intuitive to navigate than Google TV, Apple TV, or Roku. It supports all of the major streaming apps.
The Good
- Bright picture
- Vibrant color
The Bad
- Some color inaccuracy out of the box
- Very distracting reflective screen
- More blooming than competitors
Speaking of software, a quick note: LG has recently come under increased scrutiny after a video from Gamers Nexus showed security vulnerabilities and continuous audio recording on its TVs, which LG has denied. When setting up the MRGB95B, it’s only necessary to accept the terms of use and privacy policy if you want to use webOS. Otherwise, as with any TV, it can be disconnected from the internet, although an external streaming device would be needed for any streaming services (I use an Apple TV 4K, myself).
OK, moving on. So, why buy an RGB LED TV?
RGB LED TVs use zones of individual red, green, and blue LEDs as backlights as opposed to a field of white or blue LEDs that rely on a color filter or quantum dots to create the colors that reach our eyes. RGB LED TVs have a color filter, too, but since the backlight is already creating color based on what’s needed onscreen, the color filter doesn’t need to work as hard to dial that in. It allows for higher color brightness and the ability to display more colors.
LG (and Samsung) use the term Micro RGB to describe the technology, while others say Mini RGB LED. And while the LG and Samsung RGBs are reportedly smaller (although neither has confirmed the exact size), it doesn’t directly translate into more zones or better performance over Mini RGB.
As with all of the RGB LED TVs I’ve seen this year, the 95B gets very bright — I measured a peak of 4,011 nits in HDR Filmmaker mode — allowing it to deliver an impactful image even in a sunlit living room. And in a dark room, the highlights in scenes from The Meg really pop. At the other end of the spectrum, though, the LG struggles a bit. Near-black shadow detail, such as the corners of the living room and kitchen of Sapper Morton’s home at the beginning of Blade Runner 2049, is difficult to see. And when there are bright moments within a dark portion of the screen — subtitles are a good example — the LG exhibits more blooming than I’ve seen on other RGB LED TVs.
LG MRGB95B specs
Display type: RGB LED
HDR formats: Dolby Vision, HDR10, HLG
TV OS: webOS 26
HDMI inputs: 4 x HDMI 2.1 (one with eARC)
Audio support: Dolby Atmos, Dolby Atmos FlexConnect, Dolby Digital, Auracast
Gaming features: VRR, ALLM, Game Optimizer, G-Sync compatible
Sizes available (inches): 75, 86, 100
The LG 95B can display really vibrant colors thanks to the RGB LED technology. It’s able to cover 100 percent of the P3 color gamut (which is what’s used for films) and nearly 90 percent of the larger BT.2020 color area. But even in Filmmaker mode out of the box, those colors still show visible accuracy issues. Overall, the TV leans toward light blue, so white clouds have a slight blue tint to them and skin tones are cooler than they should be.
After a few days living with the LG MRGB95B, I got used to the slightly blue image (although it was still noticeable). A $3,600 TV in 2026 shouldn’t have the inaccuracies on the MRGB95B.
While the TV performs well in a bright room during the day, when the sun goes down and the lamps turn on, they can wreak havoc on the image. The 95B’s glossy coating is one of the most reflective I’ve seen in a long time. In moderately lit rooms, a lamp or ceiling light directly reflected on the screen causes rainbows to dance across the image. It’s not as bad when the scene is bright, such as the scorching desert of Arrakis in Dune, but once we enter the dark corridors of House Harkonnen, the reflections become incredibly noticeable.
Viewing angles are always a problem for LED TVs — RGB or not — and that’s evident on the LG, too. When only moderately off-axis, the colors become washed out, losing their vibrancy for anyone who’s sitting off to the side.
In a vacuum, the MRGB95B is a good TV for certain situations. It’s really bright and stands up to ambient light well (just avoid having ceiling, wall, or standing lights reflected on the screen), and the colors are vibrant if not totally accurate out of the box. But it doesn’t hold up against other TVs. The Sony Bravia 7 II (which you can find $1,300 cheaper at 75 inches) has better color accuracy and handles reflections better. And the Hisense UR9 performs comparably for less money, too.
But the real competition comes from within LG itself. The LG G6 OLED is only a few hundred dollars more than the MRGB95B, as is the Samsung S95H, and both of those TVs offer significantly better performance with superior color accuracy and viewing angles. The OLEDs don’t get quite as bright, but since they can turn off light at the pixel level, contrast is remarkable and there’s zero blooming.
LG has always struggled to make competitive LED TVs, and that trend continues with the MRGB95B. In fact, it might be LG’s best argument to get an LG OLED TV.
Photography by John Higgins / The Verge
How I test TVs
I set up each TV in my living room on my home theater credenza. I stream movies and shows through the TV’s apps and from an Apple TV 4K, play discs on my Oppo UDP-203 4K Blu-ray player (including the Spears & Munsil Ultra HD Benchmark disc), and play games on my Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5. This is done at different times of the day and under different lighting conditions, with curtains open, with lamps and overhead lights on, or with blackout curtains up to keep the room dark. While I am a certified ISF Level 3 calibrator, I do not calibrate the TVs before measurement, as the overwhelming majority of TV owners don’t bother. So it’s important to know how well the TVs perform out of the box, with minor tweaks in the menu anyone can do.
For measurement, I use Portrait Displays’ Calman color calibration software, a Murideo 8K Seven pattern generator, an X-rite i1 Pro 3 spectrophotometer, Portrait Displays’ C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a Konica Minolta LS-100 luminance meter, and Leo Bodnar 4K lag tester.

articles.title: Tesla's Full Self-Driving is now called Assisted Driving in Europe - Engadget
articles.text:
Tesla's Full Self-Driving is now called Assisted Driving in Europe
Regulators were concerned that the old name could lead people to believe that it enabled full driverless capabilities.
Tesla has changed the name of its Full Self-Driving feature in some of its European websites, including Germany, Spain and France, to "Assisted Driving." While the Full Self-Driving feature is already available in some parts of Europe, Tesla is working to get it approved in more countries. As Reuters reports, the rebranding came after Germany revealed that its Transport Minister Steffen Bilger is advocating for its swift approval. In the country's announcement, it explained that the term Full Self-Driving, particularly because it is still of the Supervised variety, is "somewhat misleading."
The system doesn't actually drive the car, Germany's Federal Ministry for Digital and Transport said, and it only provides assistance for certain tasks, like accelerating and braking. Bilger said he discussed regulators' concerns over the feature with Tesla in September and that they had reached an understanding. The automaker then agreed to rename the feature Tesla Assisted Driving. "I will now advocate for the system's timely approval across Europe," he said.
In Europe, Tesla Assisted Driving is already available in several countries, including the Netherlands, Denmark, Belgium, Slovenia, the Czech Republic and Croatia. Reuters says Swedish and Italian authorities are assessing whether the name Full Self-Driving could cause confusion among consumers and make them believe it has unsupervised driving capabilities. The rebranding could remove the hurdles Tesla is facing to be able to roll the feature out to the rest of the continent in the future.

articles.title: Salesforce renames AIForce to SIForce after Trump’s push
articles.text:
Salesforce is renaming its AIForce agent platform to SIForce, chief executive Marc Benioff said on Friday, as Katherine Li reported for Business Insider.
“The era of Super Intelligence is here. AIForce is officially SIForce,” Benioff wrote on X.
The change covers the agent platform only, not the company’s name.
Following the president’s lead
Benioff is the second big tech boss to fall in line this week. Last Sunday, Elon Musk said SpaceXAI would be renamed SpaceXSI.
Both moves follow Donald Trump’s push to replace the term artificial intelligence with super intelligence. A 29 September executive order told federal agencies to make the switch in official documents and websites.
The order does not apply to private firms. But on Thursday, Trump went further.
Anyone who still says “artificial intelligence” is “THE ENEMY,” he wrote on Truth Social.
A name is not a threshold
Superintelligence usually means systems that are far more capable than humans across many tasks. Renaming a product does not show it meets that bar, Business Insider noted.
The push also leaves firms with AI in their names, such as OpenAI and Scale AI, in an awkward spot. Neither responded to Business Insider.

articles.title: Ngân hàng rao bán nhà máy nước của doanh nghiệp có chủ tịch là ca sĩ
articles.text:
Nhà máy do Công ty Cổ phần Đặng Đoàn Nguyễn làm chủ đầu tư; bà Nguyễn Thụy Đông Đào, tức ca sĩ Đông Đào, là Chủ tịch HĐQT kiêm Tổng Giám đốc công ty.
Tài sản được rao bán gồm quyền sử dụng đất tại thửa đất số 130, tờ bản đồ số 6, tại xã Bình Khánh (xã Tam Thôn Hiệp, huyện Cần Giờ cũ), TPHCM.
Diện tích thửa đất 12.809,8m2, là đất cơ sở sản xuất, kinh doanh (xây dựng nhà máy xử lý nước lợ). Đất do nhà nước giao, có thu tiền sử dụng đất, thời hạn sử dụng đất đến hết ngày 20/10/2056.
Ngoài ra, tài sản được ngân hàng rao bán gồm toàn bộ hệ thống dây chuyền, máy móc, thiết bị của nhà máy xử lý nước lợ, dây chuyền nước đóng chai (tài sản thuộc Nhà máy nước Cần Giờ), nhà máy tại xã Bình Khánh, TPHCM (xã Tam Thôn Hiệp, huyện Cần Giờ cũ).
Giá khởi điểm của tài sản là 52,188 tỷ đồng. Trong đó, giá khởi điểm của quyền sử dụng đất là 49,326 tỷ đồng; giá khởi điểm bán đấu giá tài sản là toàn bộ hệ thống dây chuyền, máy móc, thiết bị của nhà máy là 2,862 tỷ đồng.
Giá khởi điểm đã bao gồm thuế GTGT, chưa bao gồm các loại thuế, phí liên quan đến chuyển nhượng tài sản theo quy định pháp luật.
Trong thông báo, Agribank Chi nhánh Trung tâm Sài Gòn đề nghị Công ty Cổ phần Đặng Đoàn Nguyễn và bà Nguyễn Thụy Đông Đào phối hợp chặt chẽ với đơn vị bán đấu giá.
Nhà máy nước Cần Giờ là dự án do Công ty Cổ phần Đặng Đoàn Nguyễn làm chủ đầu tư. Bà Nguyễn Thụy Đông Đào (ca sĩ Đông Đào) làm Chủ tịch HĐQT kiêm Tổng Giám đốc công ty.

articles.title: FPT gánh 2 sức ép, mất 4,5 tỷ USD vốn hóa bất chấp lợi nhuận tăng vọt
articles.text:
Cổ phiếu FPT mất hơn 38% từ đầu năm, vốn hóa bốc hơi
Phiên giao dịch ngày 9/10, cổ phiếu FPT của Tập đoàn FPT tiếp tục giảm 1.800 đồng, xuống 57.900 đồng/cp, sau một phiên chững lại. Trước đó, mã này trải qua 11 phiên giảm liên tiếp.
Từ mức 66.600 đồng/cp ngày 23/9, cổ phiếu FPT mất khoảng 13% giá trị, tương ứng gần 16.600 tỷ đồng vốn hóa. Tính từ đầu năm 2026, mã này giảm hơn 38%. So với vùng đỉnh gần 120.000 đồng/cp hồi cuối tháng 1/2025, thị giá đã giảm hơn một nửa, kéo vốn hóa doanh nghiệp giảm khoảng 117.000 tỷ đồng, tương đương gần 4,5 tỷ USD.
Áp lực đáng kể đến từ giao dịch của khối ngoại. Nhà đầu tư nước ngoài đã bán ròng khoảng 14.800 tỷ đồng cổ phiếu FPT từ đầu năm, tương đương khoảng 180 triệu cổ phiếu, trong khi đây từng là một trong những cổ phiếu tăng trưởng được nhiều quỹ đầu tư nước ngoài ưa chuộng.
Một rủi ro khác là khả năng FPT không còn đáp ứng điều kiện duy trì trong rổ VN-Diamond khi tỷ lệ sở hữu bình quân của khối ngoại giảm. Nếu không đạt, FPT có thể rời rổ. Khi đó, hoạt động cơ cấu danh mục của các quỹ ETF tham chiếu chỉ số có thể tạo thêm áp lực bán.
Đáng chú ý, đà giảm của cổ phiếu diễn ra trong khi kết quả kinh doanh vẫn tăng trưởng tích cực.
Lũy kế 8 tháng đầu năm 2026, FPT ghi nhận doanh thu 35.408 tỷ đồng, tăng 13,5% so với cùng kỳ; lợi nhuận trước thuế đạt 7.648 tỷ đồng, tăng 17,5%. Khối công nghệ mang về hơn 31.000 tỷ đồng doanh thu, tăng 16%, đóng góp 58% tổng lợi nhuận trước thuế của tập đoàn.
Riêng dịch vụ công nghệ thông tin tại thị trường nước ngoài đạt doanh thu 25.529 tỷ đồng, tăng 13,8%. Nhật Bản tiếp tục là điểm sáng với doanh thu 11.946 tỷ đồng, tăng 20,8%. Giá trị đơn hàng ký mới ở thị trường nước ngoài đạt 33.285 tỷ đồng, tăng 28,2%.
Trong 6 tháng đầu năm 2026, FPT ghi nhận lợi nhuận sau thuế của cổ đông công ty mẹ đạt hơn 5.055 tỷ đồng, tăng mạnh so với gần 4.432 tỷ đồng cùng kỳ năm trước.
Sự trái chiều giữa kết quả kinh doanh và diễn biến cổ phiếu cho thấy nhà đầu tư có thể đang đánh giá lại không chỉ lợi nhuận hiện tại, mà cả triển vọng tăng trưởng và khả năng duy trì biên lợi nhuận của FPT trong những năm tới.
Với một doanh nghiệp có thế mạnh lâu năm trong gia công phần mềm và cung cấp dịch vụ công nghệ như FPT, câu hỏi không chỉ là AI có thể thay thế bao nhiêu công việc, mà còn là tập đoàn sẽ tạo ra giá trị gì để duy trì lợi thế cạnh tranh và tăng trưởng.
AI tạo sức ép lên mô hình kinh doanh của FPT
Trong hơn ba thập kỷ, FPT xây dựng vị thế hàng đầu trong ngành công nghệ dựa trên nguồn nhân lực kỹ thuật, chi phí cạnh tranh, khả năng triển khai dự án quy mô lớn và mạng lưới khách hàng quốc tế. Từ gia công phần mềm, tập đoàn mở rộng sang chuyển đổi số, điện toán đám mây, dữ liệu và các giải pháp công nghệ cho doanh nghiệp.
Lợi thế của FPT không chỉ nằm ở năng lực phát triển phần mềm, mà còn ở khả năng tổ chức đội ngũ kỹ sư, quản lý dự án, tích hợp hệ thống và duy trì hoạt động sau bàn giao.
Tuy nhiên, AI đang thay đổi cách phát triển phần mềm. Các công cụ AI có thể hỗ trợ viết mã, kiểm thử, phân tích yêu cầu và tạo tài liệu. Những công việc trước đây cần nhiều giờ lao động của kỹ sư nhưng giờ có thể được thực hiện nhanh hơn, với chi phí thấp hơn. Điều này không đồng nghĩa kỹ sư phần mềm sẽ biến mất, nhưng có thể khiến khách hàng không còn sẵn sàng trả mức giá cũ cho những công việc phổ thông.
Rủi ro lớn nhất vì thế không đơn thuần là AI thay thế con người, mà là năng suất tăng lên khiến giá bán dịch vụ truyền thống chịu sức ép.
Trên thế giới, FPT cũng phải cạnh tranh với các tập đoàn sở hữu nền tảng điện toán đám mây, mô hình AI và hệ sinh thái phần mềm lớn, cùng các doanh nghiệp dịch vụ công nghệ và công ty phát triển sản phẩm dựa trên AI. Áp lực không chỉ nằm ở giá cả mà còn ở năng suất và tốc độ đổi mới.
FPT cũng đứng trước bài toán đầu tư dài hạn. Muốn gia tăng giá trị trong chuỗi công nghệ, tập đoàn phải mở rộng năng lực về AI, dữ liệu, bán dẫn, điện toán đám mây và an ninh mạng. Quá trình này đòi hỏi nguồn vốn và nhân lực có chuyên môn cao, trong khi các mảng dịch vụ hiện tại vẫn phải duy trì doanh thu, lợi nhuận.
Một thách thức khác là nguồn nhân lực. Kỹ sư cần được đào tạo liên tục để nâng cao năng lực thiết kế hệ thống, đánh giá kết quả do AI tạo ra và xử lý các bài toán chuyên sâu. Với những khách hàng thuộc lĩnh vực tài chính, ngân hàng, y tế hay sản xuất, yêu cầu về bảo mật, độ chính xác, quyền sử dụng dữ liệu và trách nhiệm khi xảy ra sự cố ngày càng cao.
FPT đang theo đuổi chiến lược AI-First, trong đó có nền tảng FleziPT nhằm ứng dụng AI vào quy trình phát triển phần mềm và cung cấp dịch vụ. Tập đoàn cũng có kinh nghiệm triển khai dự án phức tạp và mạng lưới khách hàng quốc tế, tạo cơ sở để mở rộng từ cung cấp dịch vụ sang hợp tác nghiên cứu, phát triển và thương mại hóa công nghệ.
Trong bối cảnh AI phát triển nhanh, thách thức của FPT là nâng cao giá trị dịch vụ và duy trì lợi thế cạnh tranh. Quy mô nhân lực cùng kinh nghiệm triển khai vẫn là những lợi thế, nhưng hiệu quả tăng trưởng sẽ phụ thuộc vào khả năng ứng dụng AI và chuyển đổi hoạt động kinh doanh.

articles.title: AI agent makers are promising privacy — will they deliver?
articles.text:
At this year’s OpenAI DevDay, CEO Sam Altman unveiled the company’s new AI agent Dots — and told the crowd that the company wants to “set a new standard for privacy in frontier AI.” OpenAI would spend the day taking veiled shots at Meta’s Muse, its primary competitor, for failing to keep users’ data safe. Yet Muse itself, a couple of months earlier, had launched as a supposedly safer alternative to predecessor OpenClaw — with CEO Mark Zuckerberg promising it was “built from the ground up for privacy and security.”
AI agent makers are promising privacy — will they deliver?
Meta positioned its Muse agent as a safer alternative to OpenClaw. OpenAI promises Dots is a safer alternative to Muse.
In an age when companies hoard customers’ personal data and cyberattacks are a dime a dozen, AI labs are trying to convince users to share even more information with their agents. Their latest strategy for success is one-upping the competition by promising that unlike their rivals, they’ll keep user data away from prying eyes. The question is whether companies can keep these promises.
Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, wrote on X that the company’s “goal with muse was to build something like openclaw that we could make safe and secure and easy to use and scale to billions of people.” User data is stored on a secure VM, what Zuckerberg described as an “isolated linux computer with a browser, CPU, memory, and storage.” The company said that most of the effort in building Muse was related to “careful design and engineering to operate [it] more safely.” Meta’s blog post continued, “Muse can and will still make mistakes, but we expect they’ll be much less frequent and cause much less damage due to the safety systems we’ve built in.”
But though Muse topped the App Store charts and, per Apptopia, gained 600,000 daily active users in the US within weeks, Meta’s promises seem to have fallen short. Although data is isolated from other users, and the company plans to introduce a way “to cryptographically and verifiably prevent Meta from accessing data in your VM” later this year, Meta itself can still access the data. A security researcher quickly exposed a zero-day vulnerability that could allow someone to take control of Muse (which has since been patched), raising fears of outside attacks. Multiple serious security issues reportedly cropped up at the last minute before launch, one of which could have allowed users to access Meta’s own internal databases, per 404 Media.
Muse also appears to liberally collect (and in some cases, hand out) data. It defaults to allowing Meta to train models on what users put into it, though it’s possible to opt out. An Inc. reporter complained that Muse uploaded and read his private messages without him asking it to, and a YouTuber said it had offered his address to a stranger via Marketplace — in both cases, Muse was functioning apparently as intended, but the user didn’t realize how far it would go. The platform creates “detailed profiles of all your friends and family,” as Wired reported. None of this is necessarily unexpected from Meta, but it certainly doesn’t back up the idea that Muse is uniquely privacy- or security-conscious.
OpenAI seized on this fact when announcing Dots in late September. Alexander Embiricos, OpenAI’s Codex product lead, said onstage at DevDay that OpenAI is focused on having the “most trustworthy, safe, and secure assistant,” and CEO Sam Altman demonstrated ways that people could exert control over their individual Dots, such as setting a rule that it should never make a purchase over a certain dollar amount. “I think we’re in a different position to Meta in that they don’t have an AI product that has 1.2 billion users,” said Glen Coates, OpenAI’s head of app platform, adding that “launching something that makes those kinds of mistakes is something that we would try to take the care to avoid.”
Altman himself also pushed the privacy angle at DevDay. To court business customers, executives presented a framework allowing enterprises to have “stronger controls” over their data and zero data retention policy options (meaning no data is stored on OpenAI servers). Indeed, so far, there haven’t been many privacy scandals with Dots — although since it’s only available on the $100-and-up ChatGPT subscription tiers, there are also likely fewer people using it.
People may still not feel comfortable giving OpenAI their personal data, in part simply because AI agents require so much of it. For instance, The Verge’s Allison Johnson felt uncomfortable typing in her bank information when the bot asked as part of a relevant task (Muse has a Stripe integration to take care of that).
Not all companies are making privacy promises, of course. Instinct was publicly criticized for reportedly overly-broad terms of service that gave it unfettered access to data; since then, the company seems to have made adjustments. For now, AI labs seem to be counting on a three-part approach to popularizing AI agent use with the general public: Make them useful, make them cute and disarming to help offset the creepiness, and make promises about privacy — and hope they hold up.

articles.title: Ramp hits $60bn valuation in $1.85bn round
articles.text:
Fintech start-up Ramp has raised about $1.85bn at a valuation of roughly $60bn, Rebecca Torrence reported for Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter.
Dragoneer Investment Group and Thrive Capital led the round, and Founders Fund also wrote a large cheque, the people said. The $60bn figure is before the new money is counted.
$16bn in four months
The deal confirms talks that Bloomberg first reported in September. Ramp raised $750mn in June at a $44bn valuation.
Founded in 2019 and based in New York, Ramp sells corporate cards and tools for expenses, payments and fraud detection.
It said in June that it worked with 70,000 businesses, up from 50,000 at the start of the year. Its annualised revenue had passed $1.5bn by then, Bloomberg reported.
The last one standing
Ramp is now by far the most valuable start-up in business spending. Its closest rival, Brex, sold to Capital One for $5.15bn earlier this year.
The company is also leaning into AI. In August, it released a tool that sends tasks to cheaper models where it can, and it is weighing training its own models.
Ramp declined to comment to Bloomberg.

articles.title: The techlash has gone Hollywood
articles.text:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 147, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, I missed you all, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
The techlash has gone Hollywood
Plus, in this week’s Installer: Amazon’s new tablet, a new book on the AI industry, Star Wars racing, and more.
I’m back from parental leave! Part time, anyway. Thanks to everyone who sent well wishes and tips for managing three kids. I need ’em all. This week, I’ve been reading about McMansions and data centers and sports cardsand ICANN, trying to run my life on the Dell XPS Googlebook, testing a new and very purple Kindle, reinventing my whole note-taking system now that Google Docs can handle Markdown files, listening to episode after episode of No Such Thing as a Fish,and watching all of Shrinkingbetween the hours of 1 and 5AM while feeding a baby.
I also have for you the new Facebook movie, a tech-related procedural, a couple of great new gadgets, the Star Wars game that is going to destroy my productivity, a terrific book about the AI industry, and much more. Let’s do this.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What have you been watching / reading / playing / listening to / putting in the air fryer this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- The Social Reckoning. My hopes were not super high for this movie, and the reaction so far suggests it’s good but a far cry from The Social Network. (Which I just watched recently, and absolutely still rips.) Still, Aaron Sorkin and Jeremy Strong will end up in the annals of Big Tech Movies, and I will not be missing this one.
- The Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. For the first time ever, Amazon decided — and I know this might sound far-fetched — to just build an awesome tablet. And it seems it may have! There’s lots of testing to do, and I’m particularly curious about this high-end model with the fancy screen, but I’m hopeful this is the “iPad but cheaper” we’ve been waiting for. For years.
- The AGI Chronicles. However bizarre you think the AI industry is, I promise Kevin Roose’s book will convince you it’s even more so. Roose has been deep inside the AI labs for the last few years, and I think came out with the most important story in AI: how a few executives, and the relationships between them, somehow came to determine the future of everything.
- Star Wars: Galactic Racer. It’s a super high-fidelity Star Wars racing game in which you (eventually) get to pilot a podracer. That’s all I needed to hear! Oh, and if you’re a Prime subscriber, you can play it for free on Amazon’s Luna service.
- Cupertino. The folks who made The Good Wife made a show about technology, and it is exactly what you think it is. I kind of love it! What I’ve seen so far is pretty thoughtful about some complicated real-life legal stuff in tech and AI, and the procedural setup is frankly a nice break from all these miniseries and four-hour docs.
- The Surface Laptop Ultra. Microsoft revealed all the details of its most impressive laptop, and while it’s expensive ($2,600!), it also looks and sounds fantastic. Microsoft is pushing the device’s AI capabilities, but this also looks like the uncompromising MacBook Pro competition a lot of Windows users might want.
- Gears of War: E-Day. When it comes to raw, brutal combat, Gears doesn’t miss very often. This one also seems to deliver on story and exploration, which aren’t always the series’ strong points; a lot of people have been waiting for the origin-story title, and I’m thrilled the game pulls it off.
- Blockers. Michael Lewis tells the story of Elon Musk and DOGE, and in particular of the government employees who tried to stop them from running roughshod over the federal government. I really enjoyed The Fifth Risk, Lewis’ last book about the government, and I expect to like this one too.
One thing about parental leave is that it involves a lot of time with one hand free. Over the last seven weeks I’ve spent dozens, maybe hundreds of hours on the couch while a tiny potato of a baby sleeps or cries or farts on top of me. So what did I do with all that time? Goofed around on my phone, mostly. Too much Reddit, too much TikTok, mercifully at least a little reading and crosswording.
I also redid my entire homescreen, because of course I did, and I figured I’d share. Here’s my current setup:
The phone: iPhone 17. I have no desire to upgrade to the 18… but I find myself hopelessly lusting after a Duo. I must not give in.
The wallpaper: Black. I am on an endless quest to make my phone less interesting to look at, and this helps. It also helps make my phone a little less blaring when I’m looking at it in the dark, which I do a lot these days.
The apps: Unread, Instapaper, Google Maps, Capacities, Daygame, Flora, Phone, Pocket Casts, Spotify, Camera, Prism, Mimestream, Arc.
A few things I want to mention here:
- The widgets at the top are Calendars and Acme Weather. Acme is a fabulous weather app, and I love the hourly widget; Calendars is, like, fine. I switch between it and Fantastical all the time. I don’t think I like any calendar app.
- The only truly new things on my homescreen are Flora and Prism. Flora is a journaling app currently in TestFlight for Apple devices, and it is fabulous. It’s simple and straightforward, but also pulls in workout data, photos, and more to give a really cool snapshot of your day. Prism is a note-taking app that is as fast as texting yourself but with many more organizational powers. I have spent forever looking for a quick, transient way to jot stuff down and organize it later; Prism might be it.
- In case you’re following my endless search for notes apps: I’m back on Capacities, which finally clicked for me. It is a project to get the app fully customized, but it turns out to work exactly like my brain does.
- I switched from Readwise Reader to Instapaper because I recently bought a Kobo, and Instapaper is so nicely integrated into the device. I like the whole setup, but also the Boox Palma 3 is coming, so my reading universe might be in for yet another overhaul soon.
- Daygame, in the middle there, is a thing I built for myself to manage all the daily games I play — it’s just a page full of links to games, which open in various apps and tabs. I might try and spruce it up and share it more widely. Send games I should include!
Before I forget, a few more recommendations from my parental leave:
- Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die. Maybe the strangest movie I watched over the last couple of months, and certainly the one that made me think the most about tech and AI and the future we’re heading toward.
- Tuner. A movie about a piano tuner who falls into a world of safecracking. Nothing I say about this movie will make it sound compelling, but I promise: It’s great.
- Furious. One of the most intense, propulsive crime shows I’ve seen in forever. Could barely put it down.
- Footnotes. A really cool (Apple-only) journaling and notes app, with emphasis on taking pictures and video right next to your notes. One of the most uniquely designed mobile apps I’ve ever used.
- Podcast Shuffle. I had no idea I needed this app until I tried it. You just press a button, and it randomly plays an episode from whatever podcast or podcasts you’ve selected. I use it for falling asleep, I use it for long drives, I love not having to scroll just to get something playing.
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky.
“Playing StarCraft II since the announcement of a new StarCraft in 2030. Just learned that macOS will drop support of Rosetta 2 in 2028 so no more StarCraft for Mac.” — Christian
“I’m going on a 13-hour road trip, once again guided solely by an old-school Garmin dashboard-mounted GPS. (DriveSmart series; I forget what size.) I like that it’s a single-purpose device with no ads, no subscriptions, and that continues to get map updates.” — sringsmuth
“The recent Hyperfixed podcast episode about the microwave popcorn button is one of the Verge-iest non Verge podcasts I’ve heard in a long time. A BUTTON IS A PROMISE.” — MrEnthusiasm
“I recently finished playing Wolverine on PS5, and I’m blown away by its incredible story and graphics. Insomniac delivered on that unspoken promise of slashing and dashing through bad guys — it feels like a whole new level for the character and for fans of Wolverine.” — Josue
“Just saw Other Mommy. It’s like a fun amusement park ride in the form of a campy horror film.” — Kevin
“I’m building a shed. The tech angle is learning new things using YouTube, online library books, and some AI reviews of local building code pdfs to check if I missed anything. I’m probably doing it all wrong, but that’s what the fire pit is for.” — Tim
“I have fallen headfirst into retro gaming on a Nintendo 3DS XL. The catalog of DS & 3DS games is absolutely massive. Running on native, easily reparable hardware, it’s hard to beat in terms of performance and cost. Ok…back to Picross 3D.” — Jacob
“The Ezra Klein interview with the ex-OpenAI guy and the Jon Stewart interview with the other ex-OpenAI guy.” — Chung
“I have been listening to World War II by Tom Hanks from the History Channel.” — Michael
Signing off
You might already know about the HTX Studio YouTube channel, but if you don’t, trust me, you need to check it out. It’s a team of makers and creators from China who are making some of the most innovative tech videos I’ve seen in years. I have watched their video about AirDesk approximately 25 times, and I want that desk more every single time I see it. The channel is a bit over a year old, and I have yet to find an HTX video that isn’t worth the time — even the one about the cow.
See you next week!

articles.title: Quinn Emanuel maps how AI data centre debt could unravel
articles.text:
A memo from US law firm Quinn Emanuel sets out how the debt behind the AI data centre boom could turn into a wave of lawsuits. Liz Hoffman reported that it was doing the rounds again this week for Semafor.
The 20-page client alert was first published in March. It is unusual because it names specific deals, Hoffman wrote.
Deals under the microscope
One is a data centre in upstate New York leased by AI cloud firm Fluidstack, with Google backing the lease. Google’s guarantee only starts once building is finished, the memo notes, so a delay could leave lenders exposed.
It also looks at the financing behind Meta’s giant Hyperion site in Louisiana, CoreWeave’s loans backed by its GPUs, and Oracle’s off-balance-sheet leases.
When chips lose value
The core worry is that AI chips lose value fast. If the GPUs used as collateral are worth less than the loans, lenders could fight over who gets paid.
Because many deals are linked, one default could spread to others. The firm calls this a risk of cascading insolvencies.
It likened GPU-backed lending to “using one’s credit card to pay off the debt on another credit card.”
Hoffman noted that Quinn Emanuel is a litigation firm. If the deals go wrong, it stands to win the court work.
The memo adds to a growing debate about how much AI debt sits off company balance sheets.

articles.title: The Telo MT1 is a big truck trapped in a tiny truck’s body
articles.text:
I’m bouncing down the road in San Carlos, California, zipping past behemoth tech companies like EA and Oracle, in America’s smallest electric truck.
The Telo MT1 is a big truck trapped in a tiny truck’s body
Tiny pickup trucks might just become a thing in the US if the California-based startup Telo has its way.
The Telo MT1 is a big truck trapped in a tiny truck’s body
Tiny pickup trucks might just become a thing in the US if the California-based startup Telo has its way.
The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now.
It has a nearly cab-over design, meaning that front-seat passengers sit almost directly over the front axle. It looks a lot like a Japanese kei truck, with a super-short nose and four doors. People stop to stare as we sit at stoplights or roll silently past.
The interior is surprisingly spacious, and while the seats are firm, they’re not uncomfortable, at least for short jaunts on the bumpy roads around Telo’s HQ. Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor.
Behind the wheel, the MT1 feels like a lighter, more nimble pickup truck with a stiff, slightly bouncy ride without any payload in the bed, combined with all the low-end power, torque, and acceleration of an EV. Once we circle back around to the road in front of Telo’s offices, Marks has me come to a full stop and stomp on the accelerator to get a feel for just how much power the little truck puts down, remarking that this was the same road where Tesla used to do its customer test drives of the Roadster many years ago.
People stop to stare as we sit at stoplights
Marks says that the production version of the Telo will accelerate 0–60mph in an estimated four seconds. The truck easily rockets from a standstill, just like any other electric vehicle on the market today, a feat for a small startup with just 30 employees.
Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area. The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market.
“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us,” Forrest North, Telo’s cofounder and CTO, said during our interview at Telo’s headquarters. “I mean, they’re fun to be up super high and look out and feel like you’re dominating the world, but they’re killing an extra, roughly, 5,000 people per year, so do we want to just give them a pass for that?”
How Telo was born
Marks and North both live and work in the San Francisco Bay Area with their families, and both own pickup trucks: Marks because he has a 150lb three-legged dog he shuttles back and forth to the office every day, and North because he has a passion for the outdoors. Large pickup trucks can be useful, but they’re far from suitable for city life. That disconnect, as well as the founders’ passion for urban transportation, is what brought the two, along with Yves Behar, together to start Telo in 2022.
Marks previously worked on automotive safety and validation at National Instruments, while North is a former battery engineer at Tesla, founder of Mission Motors (one of the first electric motorcycle companies to break the land speed record for an electric motorcycle), and cofounder of Recargo, which developed EV charging app PlugShare. Behar is the founder of fuseproject, an industrial design and brand development firm. Marks and North met through a mutual friend in the startup space and discovered they’d gone to the same high school in Washington, where they both pole-vaulted. It was a “kindred spirit moment,” according to Marks.
“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us.”
— Telo cofounder Forrest North
Originally, their idea wasn’t about trucks at all — it was about electric motorcycles. Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck. Everyone they talked to kept gravitating toward the tiny pickup. Sensing the enthusiasm, North pushed Marks to consider pivoting to building a truck, even though the motorcycle they’d planned was nearly complete. They even went so far as to poll about 200 people on the street and found that nearly 90 percent would rather have the truck. The next week, they pivoted from motorcycle to truck.
“It’s clear to me that the trucks have just kind of jumped the shark,” North said. “The only thing they can do now is be big.” Telo aims to change the conversation about what electric transportation in urban centers can look like.
Battery, range, and layout
For a small truck, the Telo MT1 packs a lot of range. At launch, the truck will come with a 77kWh battery pack, or a larger 106kWh pack that the company estimates will deliver up to 350 miles of range. The MT1 has a unique battery layout: a split pack with both 800V and 400V architecture. The 400V setup makes the Telo chargeable on Tesla’s V3 Supercharger infrastructure, while the 800V will let customers take advantage of new, higher-powered stations coming to market in areas like San Francisco.
Telo currently builds its battery packs in-house. Each cell is individually fused so that a single failure won’t trigger a cascade across the pack. According to Marks, in-house manufacturing allows them to maximize energy density and longevity — a feat that hinges on thermal management. The passive thermal management system operates while the vehicle is parked, maintaining cooler temperatures even in direct sunlight, while active liquid cooling engages only when the vehicle is running. Additionally, North noted that Telo’s latest cells deliver roughly 20 percent more energy than those they sourced just a year ago.
For a small truck, the Telo MT1 packs a lot of range
I drove one of two prototypes that Telo has been using for road testing. From the outside, the Telo looks smaller than its 152 inches of length suggest. With the lower rear section of the passenger seats (called the midgate) laid flat, you get a full-size, 96-inch truck bed.
To make up for the lack of a frunk, which most EVs have, Telo also developed a “monster” tunnel (named because, like in a kids’ story, it’s a “monster under the bed”), which passes door to door beneath the front of the truck bed. It’s accessible from either side and is large enough for a pair of roll-aboard carry-on suitcases to slide in endwise. Marks said that while they knew the front of the MT1 would be difficult to engineer, adding the monster tunnel created a tough engineering challenge because it sits exactly where the battery pack connects.
The interior is still being finalized, but Marks said that it will get two 13-inch digital displays that will support both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. The steering wheel also has small scroll wheels, but most features will be controlled through the screen interface.
How the Telo stacks up against the big trucks
Japanese kei vehicles became a White House talking point late last year when President Donald Trump invited the tiny trucks to be built in the US. But making that actually happen is far more complicated because kei vehicles don’t meet US crash safety regulations.
Marks claimed that Telo has solved this problem with a completely new front end and an innovative front hinge pillar that took nearly four years to develop and hundreds of thousands of hours of simulated crashes to verify. In the Telo, the redesigned hinge pillar does the structural job of a conventional one while also carrying the strut mount, the cross-car beam, and the dash — consolidating several separate parts into one. This allowed the company to cut the front-end part count roughly in half, Marks said.
“We pretty much threw all [the conventional crash architecture] away and had to start from scratch,” Marks said. The company’s team includes Tesla’s former head of crash safety, brought on to help tackle the new front end and completely reengineer it.
“We have effectively six crash [paths], two bumper beams and two shock structures, a completely different architecture of a hinge pillar, a completely different architecture of a torque box to distribute the energy appropriately to the various parts of the car and save that occupant compartment as much as possible,” he said, comparing the crash innovations to those in a Smartcar. “Would any other automaker say we’re going to bet the world on being able to rethink crash?”
The company’s team includes Tesla’s former head of crash safety
AI tools have made the virtual crash-testing process much more affordable for startups, and Telo recently locked in its body in white, the sheet metal shell made up of the major structural pieces of the truck (think of it like a skeleton of a vehicle). It’s currently being built by US supplier Schwab Industries in Michigan.
Marks said Telo uses AI to run virtual crash tests around the clock, averaging roughly one test per hour. The next phase of crash testing will include cutting the body in white apart for what Marks called a “quasi-static validation,” and full crash testing (slamming the vehicle and its various parts into a wall to validate the virtual testing the company has done) will start next year before Telo starts customer deliveries.
“I think it’s one of the most exciting times to start a hardware company,” North said. “It’s always been like, hardware is hard. That’s always been the cliché, and I wouldn’t say hardware is easy, but I would say it’s gotten so much easier because of software and AI.”
Pricing, delivery, and other features
The Telo MT1 will come in single-motor (rear-wheel drive) and dual-motor (all-wheel drive) layouts and offer add-ons like a solar-capable tonneau cover or camping shell. Reservations are open now for a refundable $152, and the base vehicle starts at $41,520. Marks said the company isn’t really worried about larger competitors like Ford’s upcoming midsized electric truck or Slate’s bare-bones EV because he sees their market entry as proof that a viable market exists for small electric pickup trucks.
North argued that Telo is also in a better position than either Slate or Ford right now because the company has fewer parts moving in and out of the country; it’s assembling its own battery packs and building the body in white stateside, making it largely exempt from the Trump administration’s tariffs. “The pack is the most expensive part of the vehicle build and the heart and soul of the vehicle,” Marks said, “so we had to keep it in-house.”
Marks said he’s been surprised by the volume of reservations: just over 14,000, with 70 percent of reservation-holders configuring AWD versions with the longer-range battery pack. He also noted that around 20 percent are first-time car buyers.
Telo is aiming for profitability at around 5,000 vehicles within roughly 24 months of deliveries. The company plans to get vehicles into customers’ hands sometime in 2027, depending on the validation timelines, but the MT1 still has to go through EPA and California air quality certification. Most reservations have come from places like LA, New York, the Bay Area, Seattle, Dallas, Washington, DC, Miami, and Denver, with almost everyone opting for the larger battery pack, regardless of drive configuration.
Marks pointed to Tesla as the trailblazer of EVs’ first real wave, proving electric cars could be fast, fun, and sporty. However, he believes the industry ultimately missed the chance to fully exploit their potential. Telo is tackling the problem by rethinking vehicle architecture from the ground up, returning to a “one-box” design made possible by eliminating wasted space.
Ultimately, Telo’s focus comes down to purpose, according to Marks: “What does electric enable for the experience of the user, and what value does that bring?”
While history has shown that the market isn’t kind to EV startups, in a world where giant American trucks increasingly barely fit in an average parking spot, the Telo MT1 and its creators are aiming to offer a capable electric pickup built for today’s cramped cities in the hope that Americans can get behind smaller and more capable electric vehicles.

articles.title: Cirrus Logic made rival bid for Synaptics, Bloomberg reports
articles.text:
Chipmaker Cirrus Logic made a surprise offer for Synaptics last month, trying to break up its agreed sale to Onsemi, Liana Baker and Yiqin Shen reported for Bloomberg.
Cirrus Logic is the ‘Party A’ named in an updated Synaptics filing on Thursday, people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. It is unclear whether Cirrus is still interested.
A switch to cash
Onsemi agreed to buy Synaptics in June in an all-stock deal then valued at about $7bn.
Cirrus Logic’s bid used cash and shares. In response, Onsemi changed its offer last week to $123 a share, all in cash, which values the deal at about $5.7bn.
Onsemi said at the time that it had acted after an “unsolicited competing proposal”, without naming the bidder.
The filing shows Synaptics’ board took the Cirrus bid seriously and held talks. It decided Onsemi’s revised offer was better for shareholders.
Chips for smart devices
Synaptics makes chips for touch, display and connected devices. Onsemi wants the deal to push into chips for smart devices.
Cirrus Logic, best known for audio chips in iPhones, has a market value of about $5.4bn, a little more than Synaptics’ $4.8bn. Its shares fell about 6% on Friday.
Cirrus Logic and Onsemi declined to comment to Bloomberg. The Onsemi deal is expected to close by mid-2027.

articles.title: Microsoft's Nadella says AI needs an ‘emergency brake’ that humans control
articles.text:
Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella on Saturday called for advanced artificial intelligence systems to be built with containment, independent controls and an "emergency brake" that lets authorized people pause or shut a model down mid-task.
"We need to surround non-deterministic models with strong, deterministic system design, human controls, and reliable operating procedures, and establish industry standards where existing ones are insufficient," Nadella wrote in a post on social media platform X.
"Treating frontier closed and open weight models like insider risks is a way to build such a system," he said.
Nadella's comments come amid warnings from top tech executives and researchers — including Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk — about insufficient AI safety protocols and claims that the technology is moving too fast.
An AI researcher quit Anthropic last month and accused the company, and its chief rival, OpenAI, of "gambling with our lives." Later that day, an alignment lead at Anthropic focused on AI safety said there's a greater than 10% chance that the technology could "kill all humans" within the next decade.
Conversely, President Donald Trump has repeatedly dismissed AI extinction risks and has instead emphasized that the industry needs to stay ahead of China. Trump also recently introduced a new "AI Force," led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, to help facilitate the industry and root out bad actors.
Microsoft's Nadella wrote Saturday that AI systems should be designed around "principles of observability."
They include model diversity; a human-readable footprint of the model's actions; continuous system testing; independent controls and auditability; containment; and incident disclosure, Nadella wrote.
"The most trustworthy Super Intelligence system will not be the one with the model we trust most," he wrote. "It will be the one that enables us to trust the model the least."

articles.title: Stocks saw new highs and big declines: How the volatile AI trade moved last week's market
articles.text: Stocks climbed to fresh record highs early last week, but renewed volatility in the artificial intelligence trade showed just how fickle investors can be in this market. The wheels almost came off the bus after Thursday's terrible session for tech stocks. Then came Friday's modest bounce-back rally, which proved to be enough to keep stocks in the green for the week. The S & P 500 logged a weekly gain of 1.2%, after hitting an all-time intraday high Tuesday and closing above 7,800 for the first time ever. The Nasdaq added 0.6% for the week. The tech-heavy index also closed at a record on Tuesday. Looking to balance out our AI exposure, we put more of our sizable cash pile to work Thursday, adding to three Club names: Kimberly-Clark , FedEx and Bank of New York . While elevated oil prices and interest rates continue to create uncertainty, we're selectively buying quality companies at attractive valuations rather than deploying all our cash at once. Here's a closer look at the three developments that drove last week's market action. SpaceX gives investors more reasons to buy into the bull case SpaceX gave investors plenty to be excited about last week. The Financial Times reported late Tuesday that the Elon Musk rocket and AI company is looking to raise $40 billion to buy more Nvidia chips and expand its AI compute business, which rents capacity to customers including Anthropic and Alphabet's Google. For Jim, the potential debt raise is a win for both companies, reinforcing the idea that Nvidia customers are generating strong returns on their AI investments. "Why not [do it]? Musk can immediately monetize these chips," Jim said. "SpaceX could end up being Nvidia's largest client at this pace. That's fantastic news for both sides." On Thursday evening, SpaceX announced a deal to acquire a nationwide spectrum portfolio , potentially positioning its Starlink service as a more formidable competitor to traditional U.S. wireless carriers. The spectrum would help address a key technical hurdle in Starlink's mobile ambitions and eventually allow SpaceX to combine satellite coverage with a ground-based network. The news slammed telecom stocks Friday and opened another potential avenue for growth beyond rockets, satellites, and AI infrastructure for SpaceX. Wall Street is taking notice. Goldman Sachs on Tuesday raised its SpaceX price target to $230 from $220, reinforcing Jim's view that the company's ambitious growth plans are becoming more tangible . Barclays initiated coverage of SpaceX in a note released late Thursday, writing that it's "the name to own in space due to its complete dominance of each vertical it operates in." While Jim still feels that SpaceX isn't appropriate for the Club portfolio, he said the developments suggest Musk's vision could become reality sooner than investors expected. OpenAI rattles the AI trade, and reinforces a key investing lesson AI stocks whipsawed last week after a Financial Times report raised questions about OpenAI's growth. The report suggested OpenAI's annualized revenue at the end of September was roughly $20 billion below what was believed to be previously indicated levels, sending AI stocks sharply lower Thursday. Club holding Broadcom fell 4.4% (though ended the week higher). Beaten-down stocks outside the AI trade rallied Thursday as Treasury yields eased. The AI trade rebounded Friday after sources told Bloomberg that OpenAI expects annualized revenue of at least $70 billion by the end of the year. The reversal underscored how quickly sentiment toward AI stocks can shift, even as the underlying demand for computing power remains strong. Jim said the real problem is that people think of AI as a trade, not an investment. For us, the bigger lesson is the importance of diversification . "If you had nothing but artificial intelligence stocks, [Thursday] would've been a nightmare," Jim said. The danger of a concentrated portfolio is that steep losses could prompt investors to panic, sell their holdings and retreat to cash, potentially missing a subsequent recovery . A diversified portfolio can help cushion losses when a particular investing theme gets hit and make it easier to stay invested. Starbucks' turnaround gains traction with consumers New consumer data offered encouraging evidence that the Starbucks turnaround is, indeed, taking hold. According to HundredX, Starbucks was the only chain among a group including Dunkin', Dutch Bros and 7 Brew to see improving customer intentions to spend more in recent months. Feedback from 29,000 customers also showed Starbucks gaining ground against competitors on taste, speed, quality, and brand trust. The findings are particularly encouraging given concerns that fast-growing beverage chains such as Dutch Bros and 7 Brew could threaten Starbucks' long-term growth. They also suggest the underlying business is improving even as worries about consumer spending have pressured restaurant stocks. A separate development, however, has complicated things. The Financial Times reported that Starbucks has explored acquiring Chipotle , raising questions about a potential deal . This is interesting because Brian Niccol engineered a successful turnaround as CEO of Chipotle before he left to try to repeat that magic as CEO of Starbucks. We're not convinced a transaction will happen. Jim said Thursday he had considered buying more shares following the sell-off. During Friday's Morning Meeting , he said a further decline to $90, coupled with signs that Starbucks won't pursue Chipotle, could present an attractive buying opportunity. He reminded members that the Club was restricted from trading because he had discussed it on CNBC on Friday. (Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust is long NVDA, AVGO, SBUX, KMB, FDX, BNY. See here for a full list of the stocks.) As a subscriber to the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer, you will receive a trade alert before Jim makes a trade. Jim waits 45 minutes after sending a trade alert before buying or selling a stock in his charitable trust's portfolio. If Jim has talked about a stock on CNBC TV, he waits 72 hours after issuing the trade alert before executing the trade.
